source.title: Benchmarking Vision Language Model Unlearning via Fictitious Facial Identity Dataset
source.authors: Ying-Zi Ma; Jiong-Xiao Wang; Fei Wang; Si-Yuan Ma; Jiazhao Li; Jin-Sheng Pan; Xiujun Li; Fu-Rong Huang; Li-Chao Sun; Bo Li; Yejin Choi; Muhao Chen; Chaowei Xiao

record.file_problem: Text contains the full paper and appendices; some tables are flattened in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests VLM unlearning efficacy and robustness using a new benchmark and measures, including paraphrased-question privacy extraction; it does not reproduce the claim’s LLM settings or attacks such as quantization or activation ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper tests paraphrased-question extraction (APE) and membership inference after unlearning. Its two-stage fine-tuning is used to implant the fictitious knowledge before unlearning; it is not a post-unlearning relearning attack. No post-unlearning small-set fine-tuning attack, activation-direction ablation, or quantization test is reported.
record.test_reason: This is a new setting: VLMs (LLaVA-Phi-mini-3B, Llama-3.2-Vision-11B) fine-tuned on fictitious facial identities, then unlearned with GA, GD, KL or PO. It reports forgetting against utility (A), a membership-inference signal showing PO refuses without deleting (C), and a paraphrased-question extraction attack (E). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find all four baselines limited, with a utility vs forget-quality trade-off. PO's low EM but high MIA shows refusal without true forgetting, so privacy attacks are needed for robust evaluation. They do not separately interpret APE; the table shows paraphrasing recovers little.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates VLM unlearning after a controlled fine-tuning stage on fictitious face-and-profile data. It tests GA, GD, KL, and PO, and adds MIA and paraphrased-question extraction; it does not test the claim’s post-unlearning recovery edits or quantization.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary with unlearning method, number of unlearning steps, forget-set size, and which VLM components are fine-tuned. The authors say more unlearning steps improve forgetting but reduce utility for GA, GD, and KL; larger forget sets make forgetting easier but can further reduce utility.

fits_no_version.finding: Which VLM components are updated during unlearning changes the trade-off. With GD on 3B, LLM-only keeps utility but forgets poorly (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: VLM unlearning efficacy depends on which modules (vision encoder, projector, LLM) are updated.

fits_no_version.finding: Forget-set size matters: a 1% forget set is hard to forget; at 10%, GA-based methods forget fully but utility drops to ~20% (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning difficulty and utility cost scale with forget-set size.

record.problems: The benchmark simulates rare knowledge by fine-tuning before unlearning and does not cover knowledge acquired during pretraining or in-context learning, as the authors note. The default forget set is 5% of identities. Some table values are flattened in the supplied text, making per-model assignment of attack metrics uncertain.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports additional model utility and forget-quality metrics for multiple methods and models. They are not all separately transcribed because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably associate every value with its model, method, and metric; r1 and r2 retain the textually stated outcomes. Figures 2–4 show sweeps over unlearning steps, forget-set sizes, and utility/forget-quality trade-offs, but their figure-only values were not added as separate rows.

untested.parts: Unrelated-example recovery attacks; knowledge acquired in pretraining (authors' stated limitation).
Activation-direction ablation; only MIA-based evidence of retained knowledge.
Jailbreaks, other languages, in-context information; only three GPT-4o paraphrases per question.
Entirely: no robust counter-method tested against attacks (KU is a data-availability variant, not a robustness claim).

missing.what: Per-model, per-method EM, MIA and APE numbers (APE vs EM comparison) for both VLMs
Over unlearning steps, PO EM drops sharply while MIA stays limited; GA/GD/KL trade utility for forgetting
Forget-split sweep (1/5/10%); PO refuses but fails to remove knowledge from internal representation

record.verdict_notes: The Table 2 column assignment is reconstructed from the flattened value order. Five-value groups map to Rouge, GPT and Truth for 3B, then Rouge and GPT for 11B, then the forget metrics. Researchers should verify against the PDF. The knowledge was implanted by fine-tuning on fictitious data, not acquired in pretraining. The Retain model's EM (~13–15) is the effective floor.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish that targeted accuracy reaches near chance while general ability is retained under the claim’s criteria; it evaluates utility and forget-quality metrics and attack robustness for its VLM setting. Does not test the claim’s unrelated-example recovery attack.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis testing access-blocking versus deletion is reported.
Tests adversarial paraphrases of questions, not jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the listed attacks.

rows.subject: LLaVA-Phi-mini-3B and Llama-3.2-Vision-11B (reported together in the authors’ general conclusion)
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned on the fictitious facial identity VQA data before unlearning
rows.operation_detail: Compared four unlearning baselines on model utility and forget quality; the authors report that none achieved good performance considering both.

conditions.value: Gradient Ascent, Gradient Difference, KL Minimization, Preference Optimization
authors’ aggregate conclusion across evaluated baselines

rows.measure: Joint model utility and forget quality
rows.baseline: Retain Model, fine-tuned on the retain set only, used as a reference in Table 2
rows.value: None of the four baseline methods achieved good unlearning performance considering both model utility and forget quality.
rows.note: The authors describe a utility/forget-quality trade-off: GA and GD give high forget quality while substantially degrading utility; KL and PO preserve utility better but struggle to forget the targeted knowledge. This does not directly establish near-chance target accuracy.
rows.check: Version code V1 is invalid; it should be A. Values are readable from Table 2, with columns inferred from the flattened order. GA on 3B: EM 14.0 vs Retain 13.3, but utility avg 42.5 vs 88.6. KL on 3B keeps utility (78.2) but EM stays 41.2. No method gets both.

rows.subject: LLaVA-Phi-mini-3B and Llama-3.2-Vision-11B (PO result described for the evaluated models)
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned on fictitious facial identity data, then Preference Optimization unlearning
rows.operation_detail: Compared Exact Match and membership-inference results after Preference Optimization; the method trains refusal responses for forget-set questions.
rows.measure: Exact Match and membership-inference measure of retained private knowledge
rows.value: The authors report substantially low EM but high MIA for PO, interpreting this divergence as evidence that private knowledge persists despite refusal behavior.
rows.note: Authors state that PO can make the model refuse while not truly removing the private knowledge. The table’s flattened layout prevents confidently assigning all displayed numeric entries to model-method-metric combinations.
rows.check: Version codes V1/V5 are invalid. MIA is not prompting, so the row bears on A and C, not E. Table 2 (inferred), PO: 3B EM 6.90 but MIA 64.2 vs Retain 12.3; 11B EM 0.30 but MIA 42.3 vs 12.2. For C this is observed: refusal without deletion. Against A, PO forgets on EM but not on MIA.

relationships.condition: All four baselines, both VLMs, default 5% split
relationships.reason: No method both forgets and keeps utility (r1). GA/GD reach Retain-level EM only with large utility loss; KL keeps utility but EM stays high. Authors say none achieve good performance.
relationships.display_finding: GA and GD reduced target exact match only with large utility losses, while KL preserved utility but left target exact match high.

relationships.reason: PO pushes EM below Retain while keeping more utility, but MIA stays far above Retain (64.2/42.3 vs ~12). Forgetting holds only on output-based measures (r2).

relationships.display_finding: Low exact match coexists with high membership-inference performance across training steps and split sizes, suggesting knowledge persists behind refusals.

tranche.reason: A new setting (VLMs fine-tuned on fictitious faces) with results on the claim. The reader's T2 fits less well because the methods are standard baselines.

source_check.notes: Table 2 is flattened. Columns checked by arithmetic: MU Avg is the mean of Rouge, GPT, Truth and ACC, and 3B FQ Avg fits the App. D.3 formula. The Retain model's EM of about 14 is the no-knowledge floor. 11B utility is Rouge 88.8 (Retain) vs KL 55.6. r2's single 'observed' state fits C; for A it reads as partial. The knowledge is fine-tuned in, not pretrained.

statements.correction: FIUBench PO: 3B EM 6.90, APE 6.80, MIA 64.2 (Retain 12.3); 11B EM 0.30, APE 0.50, MIA 42.3 (Retain 12.2). Authors: PO refuses, but the private knowledge is not fully unlearned.
statements.problem: The statement cites r2 but names no result from this study. In r2, PO's knowledge persists in likelihoods (MIA). It is not answerable by another route: paraphrases do not extract it.

statements.correction: EM to APE. 3B: GA 14.0 to 15.4, GD 18.9 to 19.0, PO 6.90 to 6.80. 11B: GA 1.60 to 1.30, GD 21.9 to 23.4, PO 0.30 to 0.50, KL 4.50 to 11.4 (Retain APE 14.3). The authors do not interpret APE.
statements.problem: None. For context, KL 11B's APE of 11.4 stays below the Retain model's 14.3. KL 3B was not forgotten (EM 41.2), so it is rightly left out.

reader_labels.condition: Evaluated VLM baselines under the default 5% forget split
reader_labels.reason: The reported trade-off means the methods did not jointly deliver strong forgetting and preserved utility; the paper does not show near-chance targeted performance with retained general ability (r1, r2).
